PullRequest.Title: Improve worktree cleanup progress, preservation, and leftover-folder handling
PullRequest.Body:
Worktree Cleanup waits for every scan and drops worktrees whose measurements exceed ten seconds. It also hides archived worktrees before background deletion has reclaimed their storage. Forced deletion can discard dirty work, while retries can run Git commands in leftover folders that are no longer registered checkouts.

The editor now shows worktrees immediately and fills in sizes independently, with a calculating state while scans are pending; finished rows without usable sizes are omitted from the table. Completed eligible rows can be selected while other scans continue, and incoming results preserve manual selection changes. Opening the editor invalidates cached measurements; there is no additional Refresh button. Failed measurements remain distinct from missing storage in the service data, including for archived sessions. Newly submitted cleanup rows show text-only “Cleaning up…” progress while their storage is rechecked individually. Completed rows disappear automatically, without reopening the editor. These checks only measure the submitted worktrees and stop after a bounded wait; retained archived rows show “Worktree still present”. Two concurrent scans and caching remain; the arbitrary per-worktree deadline is removed.

Deletion adopts the GitHub app's core preservation and residue-cleanup approach:
- Before forced removal of a registered dirty checkout, capture non-ignored working files using a temporary index and save a commit under an append-only refs/vscode-preserved-worktrees reference. The checkout's branch and index are unchanged by this snapshot. Preservation failure aborts removal; the recovery ref and command are logged.
- Check exact Git registration before running archive status/commit commands, so deregistered residue cannot accidentally commit changes in a containing repository.
- Remove residue only after confirming deregistration. Reject symlinks, non-directory replacements, and paths that contain the repository root.
- Keep a still-registered checkout whose missing .git metadata prevents preservation. Do not discard its remaining files merely to make cleanup succeed.

Existing automatic retention and mark-as-done criteria are unchanged. Recovery refs currently surface through logs rather than the GitHub app's dedicated recovery toast.

Validation: client build and type check, targeted ESLint, 61 cleanup editor/service tests, 37 automatic lifecycle tests, 12 protocol measurement tests, 132 worktree isolation/backend cleanup tests, and 9 real-Git deletion integration tests passed. Coverage includes incremental sizes, selection preservation, slow scans, failed measurements, remeasuring after cleanup, dirty-work recovery, failed-preservation aborts, missing metadata, replacement symlinks, and confirmed deregistration.

Manual testing: open Worktree Cleanup with multiple large checkouts and verify rows appear before all sizes finish. Uncheck a row and verify later results preserve the choice. Reopen the editor after cleanup to update storage. In a disposable repository, remove a dirty worktree and verify its non-ignored files remain recoverable through the logged preservation ref. Never use a valuable checkout as a destructive test fixture.


Review follow-up: removed the protocol handler’s separate ten-second cancellation deadline and tested a thirty-second request through that handler. Explicit cancellation, transport disconnection, and the shared two-scan budget remain covered. Added exact one-day boundaries for automatic marking and its additional permanent-deletion grace period; the lifecycle policy itself is unchanged.




Follow-up performance fixes: cleanup rechecks back off (at most three within 30 seconds), intermediate table renders are coalesced, and a shared measurement is canceled when its last caller cancels. Opening the editor no longer starts an additional background refresh. Directory traversal speed and concurrency are unchanged. Verified with 61 cleanup tests and the client type check.

### Latest UI and performance follow-up

- Reuse rows by session ID during progressive measurement. Changed rows update in place and existing DOM rows are moved only when the normal size ordering changes, avoiding full-table teardown and preserving selection and focus more reliably.
- Pin the displayed order after cleanup starts. Cleanup remeasurement can shrink a worktree before it disappears; those size changes now update the row without making the list jump, and completed rows are removed in place.
- Active sessions and sessions waiting for input are available for explicit manual selection but remain unchecked by default. Running and other protected sessions remain disabled. Select All and automatic/background cleanup still include only normally eligible sessions.
- Omit the storage-reclaim suffix when the selectable total is zero, avoiding summaries such as “reclaiming about 0B.”
- CPU work remains bounded: Agent Host disk walks retain the shared concurrency limit of two, abandoned shared scans are canceled, intermediate renders are coalesced, and post-cleanup verification performs at most three rescans during the 30-second progress window.

Latest validation: client transpilation, targeted ESLint, and 61 focused cleanup editor/service tests passed. Manual testing in the PR's Code OSS Agents window confirmed the summary, manual-only selection, row reuse, and stable cleanup ordering.

Findings.ConfidenceRationale: DOM appendChild semantics, the progressive callback frequency, the full-row loop, and the subsequent geometry reads are explicit. Device-specific frame cost is uncertain, but the repeated O(N×R) mutation/layout mechanism is not.
Findings.PerformanceResource: Existing DOM row nodes plus synchronous browser style/layout work from scrollWidth and scrollHeight reads
Findings.PerformanceScaling: For N visible sessions and R progressive renders, this loop performs N appendChild mutations per render even when order is unchanged, for O(N×R) DOM work (up to O(N²) as sessions finish); updates are only capped at one render per 100 ms.
Findings.PerformanceOutcome: Repeated main-thread DOM mutation and forced layout can increase interaction latency and cause dropped frames while the cleanup table is progressively populated.
Findings.PreviousBehavior: The editor waited for all measurements and built the table once, so it incurred one O(N) row insertion/layout pass.
Findings.ChangedBehavior: Progressive snapshots now call renderRows repeatedly; although rows are cached by session ID, this added line appends every cached element on every pass. appendChild moves an already attached node, and renderRows then calls updateScrollDimensions, which synchronously reads container.scrollWidth/scrollHeight after those writes.
Findings.CausalDiffEvidence: Added line 505 unconditionally re-appends each reused row inside the new progressive render loop; before the PR there were no intermediate table renders.
Findings.Title: Avoid reattaching every row on each measurement update
Findings.Impact: Opening Worktree Cleanup with dozens or hundreds of sessions while measurements finish over time repeatedly moves the entire table and forces layout, making the visible editor jank even when only one row's size changed.
Findings.Evidence: The service publishes an initial N-row snapshot and another snapshot after each measured session. The editor coalesces those to 100 ms, but renderRows sorts all visible rows, executes line 505 for every row unconditionally, then reads scroll dimensions. The signature guard avoids cell updates but does not avoid these DOM moves.
Findings.Recommendation: Reconcile order conditionally: walk the desired sequence and use insertBefore only when a row is not already at the expected sibling, skipping structural DOM writes when order is unchanged; update scroll dimensions once after an actual structural change.

Findings.ConfidenceRationale: The complete call path, fixed concurrency of two, per-worktree boundary cardinality, recursive I/O, and removed cancellation deadline are explicit in code. Exact prevalence and stall duration vary by checkout and filesystem, which affects severity rather than mechanism confidence.
Findings.PerformanceResource: Two globally limited recursive filesystem scans, each issuing directory opens and batches of file lstat calls
Findings.PerformanceScaling: One measurement is issued per distinct session worktree (and sequentially per additional worktree in a session); if the first two roots are very large or an opendir/lstat stalls, all remaining N-2 measurements wait for their full duration with no upper bound.
Findings.PerformanceOutcome: The cleanup editor and background cleanup-suggestion scan can remain pending indefinitely, with later small worktrees starved and filesystem I/O continuing for the lifetime of the caller.
Findings.PreviousBehavior: Both this protocol handler and the cleanup service canceled a per-worktree measurement after 10 seconds, which released the AgentHostWorktreeDiskUsageService's shared two-slot limiter and allowed queued worktrees to progress.
Findings.ChangedBehavior: The diff removes the protocol watchdog and the service's raceTimeout; requests now stop only on explicit caller cancellation, editor close when it is the last consumer, disconnect, or service disposal.
Findings.CausalDiffEvidence: Deleted line 3608 previously scheduled cancellation after 10,000 ms; the changed handler now awaits the recursive measurement without any deadline, while the same diff removes the matching service timeout.
Findings.Title: Prevent slow scans from monopolizing the shared scan queue
Findings.Impact: With two huge checkouts or stalled filesystem operations at the front of the scan, every later row stays in “Calculating…” and the hourly background measurement never reaches the remaining sessions; this is especially realistic for large generated trees or slow/mounted storage.
Findings.Evidence: SessionWorktreeCleanupService queues sessions with concurrency 2 and calls getSessionWorktreeDiskUsage; the provider sends one protocol request per distinct worktree. AgentHostWorktreeDiskUsageService applies another process-wide Limiter(2), and measureWorktreeDiskUsage recursively awaits opendir/lstat. Removing line 3608 eliminates the final time bound on those occupied slots; the same PR also deletes WORKTREE_MEASUREMENT_TIMEOUT_MS/raceTimeout in the caller.
Findings.Recommendation: Preserve eventual results without queue starvation by time-slicing traversal across requests (release/reacquire the shared budget between bounded directory batches); if that is not feasible, retain a bounded watchdog with an explicit failed/pending state so one root cannot hold a global slot indefinitely.

Scenarios.Scenario: Open Worktree Cleanup and progressively measure all session worktrees
Scenarios.CriticalPath: The first table snapshot is local and immediate, but usable sizes, final ordering, selection totals, and scan completion depend on the per-session disk measurements. Each progressive snapshot reaches renderRows on the visible UI path.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Send vscode/measureWorktreeDiskUsage for each distinct worktree URI
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: W requests on a cold/forced scan; multiple URIs in one session are sequential, while at most two sessions are active.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The same per-worktree protocol fan-out existed, but each measurement was canceled after 10 seconds.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Each row's size waits for its session's requests; final scan completion waits for all W.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Recursively opendir every directory and lstat regular files in batches
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One full traversal per distinct worktree on a cold scan; no worktree-level cache below the service's one-hour aggregate cache.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Traversal existed, but service and protocol watchdogs bounded each occupied slot to 10 seconds.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Occupies one of two global slots until the entire root completes; after the diff there is no deadline, so two slow roots block all queued rows.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: N sessions containing W distinct worktree URIs. The service queues at most two sessions; each provider call measures that session's distinct worktrees sequentially. Progressive UI cost scales with N visible rows and R coalesced completion snapshots.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: SessionWorktreeCleanupService uses Limiter(2); AgentHostWorktreeDiskUsageService independently enforces a process-wide Limiter(2). Intermediate UI renders are coalesced to at most one per 100 ms, but each render traverses and re-appends all visible rows.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: Opening the editor passes forceRefresh=true, invalidating the one-hour measurement cache. Concurrent callers with the same session signature coalesce onto one measurement. Closing the last progressive caller cancels it, unless a background consumer still owns the shared scan.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: the per-worktree call chain, both two-slot limiters, removed deadlines, progressive callback cadence, unconditional appendChild loop, and synchronous geometry reads are explicit.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Typical worktree counts and filesystem latency vary; large generated trees and slow or mounted filesystems determine whether starvation lasts seconds or indefinitely. Layout cost depends on row count and hardware.
Scenarios.Verdict: Reportable: removing both deadlines permits queue starvation, and progressive rendering unconditionally reattaches all N rows before a forced layout on each coalesced snapshot.

Scenarios.Scenario: Background storage-cleanup suggestion scan when the Agents window opens or sessions change
Scenarios.CriticalPath: The scan is off the window's primary startup critical path, but the suggestion cannot update until every measurement completes and its filesystem work competes for the shared Agent Host scan budget.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Request aggregate disk usage for each worktree
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: W protocol requests per cold hourly/signature scan.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Same requests, but stalled requests were canceled after 10 seconds.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Blocks suggestion calculation, though not initial window rendering.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: W traversals, globally limited to two.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Each traversal was bounded by the deleted service/protocol cancellation timers.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Two unbounded traversals can prevent the background scan and all later shared measurement requests from finishing.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: All sessions with worktrees, with effective cardinality W distinct worktree URIs across those sessions.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Two session measurements in the client and two process-wide traversals in Agent Host. The activation consumer uses CancellationToken.None, so it remains an owner until completion or service disposal.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: Cold on initial activation or after session-signature changes; otherwise the one-hour positive cache avoids repeat traversal. Failures are not cached as successful sizes, and a changed signature starts/retries measurement.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: activation at window construction, one-hour cache, CancellationToken.None ownership, and global limiter behavior are directly traced.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: The setting may be disabled and most local trees finish quickly; exact contention depends on tree size and filesystem behavior.
Scenarios.Verdict: Reportable as part of the unbounded-scan finding because this long-lived consumer can retain both shared slots even when no cleanup editor remains open.

Scenarios.Scenario: Select worktrees for cleanup, archive sessions, and verify that storage disappears
Scenarios.CriticalPath: The confirmation and sequential archiveSession calls must finish before the editor reports cleanup started. Actual Agent Host removal is scheduled in the background. The editor then performs targeted verification scans; row disappearance waits for those checks but cleanup scheduling does not.

ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The same sequential archive scheduling existed.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: On the foreground scheduling path before success is announced.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Check registration, preserve dirty work through Git status/tree/ref operations, and remove each worktree
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: Per registered forced removal: one new worktree-list check, one capture status plus tree/index resolution, optional commit-tree/update-ref for dirty content, followed by existing removal/verification commands. Cleanup pass is sequential.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Forced removal proceeded directly to git worktree remove/verification without a preservation capture.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Background storage reclamation waits for these commands; foreground archive scheduling does not.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Remeasure only selected archived worktrees still reporting storage
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: At most three scans per still-present selected worktree during 30 seconds; completed removals usually make later checks cheap or eliminate them.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The editor reloaded rather than performing bounded targeted post-cleanup checks.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Controls progress-row disappearance only; it is off the actual removal critical path.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: K selected sessions/worktrees. Verification is limited to still-archived cached rows with prior size greater than zero and retries at most three times within 30 seconds.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Archive requests are sequential. Agent Host processes pending removals sequentially in its cleanup pass. Verification scans use Limiter(2), and backend scans remain globally limited to two.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: The initial measured snapshot is reused. refreshPendingCleanup updates only selected pending IDs in the cache; removed rows become negative by omission. No full refresh is started, and checks stop after the bounded progress window.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High for subprocess and scan cardinality; actual duration is workload-dependent.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Git preservation cost depends on repository size and dirty paths; verification usually sees a missing root quickly after successful cleanup.
Scenarios.Verdict: No additional finding: preservation is an intentional safety tradeoff on a serialized background path, and verification is targeted, concurrency-limited, and retry-bounded.

Scenarios.CriticalPath: Lifecycle policy schedules pending removals; Agent Host cleanup serially processes due rows. Permanent deletion or storage reclamation completes only after registration checks, preservation where applicable, Git removal, and residue validation.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: List/read/update pending removal and co-owner state
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: A bounded sequence per due row plus one list per pass.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Same persisted cleanup queue and backoff.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Serially precedes and records each background removal.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: git worktree list, status/tree preservation, branch/state checks, remove/prune, and de-registration verification
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: Several Git subprocesses per due registered worktree; residue takes registration/prune verification without status/commit in the containing repository.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: No initial exact-registration gate and no forced-removal preservation capture; archive mode already performed branch/status/commit checks.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Determines when each serialized cleanup row can complete.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: lstat/realpath safety checks and recursive rm for confirmed deregistered residue
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One safety-check sequence and at most one recursive deletion per residual worktree.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Residual recursive deletion lacked the new canonicalization/symlink/root checks.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: On the background removal critical path only after Git confirms de-registration.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Number of due pending removal rows, processed one at a time; each row corresponds to one recorded worktree, with detached/co-owned variants separately recorded.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: The cleanup pass awaits each pending removal sequentially and per-owner/path sequencers prevent overlapping work on the same worktree.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: No measurement cache governs Git removal. Failed removals are persisted with exponential backoff. Registration checks are fresh subprocess calls, and preservation refs are append-only only when captured content differs from HEAD.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: persisted sequencing, subprocess placement, residue checks, and backoff are explicit.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: The number of due automatic removals and repository sizes vary; the serial scheduler bounds aggregate subprocess pressure.
Scenarios.Verdict: No additional finding: new boundary work is serialized and tied to preservation/safety semantics; no concurrency burst or unbounded retry was introduced.

Analysis.Summary: Completed the performance pass over all 20 changed files and paginated patches. Submitted two findings: unbounded recursive scans can starve the shared two-slot queue, and progressive table updates reattach every row before synchronous layout reads. Git preservation and targeted cleanup verification add work but remain serialized or bounded and do not independently meet the regression threshold.
